hero.title: 📖 Book Title Generator
hero.tagline: Titles for novels and stories in ten genres, each shaped the way that genre names its books.

article.intro: A title tells a browser what kind of book they're holding before they read a word of the blurb: a village murder, a dragon, a summer by the sea. This **book title generator** makes titles in ten genres, from fantasy and cosy crime to picture books and YA, using the shapes each genre's shelves are full of.

sections.heading: Eight good book titles
sections.content:
All eight came from the generator, one from each of eight genres:

  • Heir of Embers: fantasy in three words, with a person, a birthright and a hint of fire.
  • The Mistletoe Clause: a romcom you can picture from the title alone, with a deal that will obviously go wrong by Christmas.
  • Murder at the Lido: cosy crime the classic way, with a crime, a place and a seaside setting that sounds too nice for a body.
  • The Helpful Lodger: a domestic thriller where the friendly word is the frightening one.
  • What the Water Took: horror that leaves the worst part unsaid.
  • The Halcyon Protocol: sci-fi with a codename and a sense that something has been planned.
  • Milo and the Runaway Rocket: a children's book with a hero, a problem and a word that's fun to read aloud.
  • The Lacemaker's Daughter: historical fiction built on a trade and a family tie, a shape readers of the genre know well.

sections.heading: Every genre has its own title shape
sections.content:
Readers scan shelves and thumbnails fast, so genres settle into patterns that signal what's inside. The generator follows them:

  • Fantasy likes an object or person "of" an invented place, or two elements joined with "and". Real examples: Shadow and Bone (Leigh Bardugo) and A Court of Thorns and Roses (Sarah J. Maas).
  • Cosy crime names the crime and the setting: a village plus Murders, or "Death at" somewhere genteel. Richard Osman's The Thursday Murder Club is the best-known recent one.
  • Thrillers often put an ordinary person somewhere specific, as in The Girl on the Train (Paula Hawkins) and The Woman in the Window (A. J. Finn), or describe them with one unsettling word.
  • Romance sets a season at a cosy place, or names the trope: the deal, the bet, the fake date.
  • Children's books love a name and a thing (Charlie and the Chocolate Factory) or an animal who did something (The Tiger Who Came to Tea).
  • Literary fiction goes quieter: a family name, a small noun, or "What the river knew".

Those real titles are examples only; the generator checks its own results against a list of famous books and leaves them out.

sections.heading: Can someone else have the same title?
sections.content:
Yes, and it happens all the time. In the UK and the US a title on its own isn't protected by copyright, so two books can share one. A series name can be registered as a trade mark, though, and a title that copies a famous book will confuse readers and bury yours in search results.

Before you commit, search the title on Amazon, Goodreads and a library catalogue. If several books already use it, add a word or swap one: the generator's halves mix well. This is general information, not legal advice.

sections.heading: Tips for picking the one
sections.content:
• Check it as a thumbnail. Most people first see a cover the size of a stamp, so short titles read best.
  • Say it out loud. Readers recommend books by saying the title, so it should be easy to say and spell.
  • Match the genre. A romance called The Pale Choir will find the wrong readers.
  • Keep a list. Generate a few batches, star the ones you like, then sleep on it. The one you still like in the morning is usually right.

For the people inside the book, try the Character Name Generator or the Pen Name Generator for the name on the cover.

faqs.question: How do I come up with a title for my book?
faqs.answer: Choose your genre and generate a few batches, then mix halves of the ones you like. Titles that name a person, a place or a promise (a murder, a summer, a secret) tell readers fastest what they're getting.

faqs.question: What is a good title for a fantasy book?
faqs.answer: Something with a person or object and an invented place, like Heir of Embers or The Wardens of Highcairn. Choose Fantasy; the place names are made up, so they won't clash with anyone else's world.

faqs.question: What is a good title for a children's book?
faqs.answer: A name and an adventure works well, like Milo and the Runaway Rocket, or an animal who does something, like The Hedgehog Who Built a Rocket. Choose Children's for more.

faqs.question: Can I use a book title that already exists?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, as titles alone generally aren't protected by copyright in the UK or US. But a title shared with a well-known book will confuse readers, so search before you publish and pick one that stands out.

faqs.question: Does it work for short stories and fan fiction?
faqs.answer: Yes. Short stories suit the shorter titles, such as What the Water Took or Notes on Leaving. Choose Any genre for a mix, or the genre your story fits.

faqs.question: Are these real book titles?
faqs.answer: They're made up and checked against a list of famous books, so you won't get Gone Girl or The Hobbit. A smaller book may still share one by chance, which is why a quick search is worth it.
